title: A pharmaceutical client must remove drug residues (diclofenac, carbamazepine) that our biological step doesn't catch.

record.text: A pharmaceutical client must remove drug residues (diclofenac, carbamazepine) that our biological step doesn't catch.
record.detail: One of our pharmaceutical clients — a generics manufacturer in Sremska Mitrovica — must meet a discharge limit for active pharmaceutical ingredients before their permit renewal in late 2026. Right now our MBR system handles the biological oxygen demand fine, but two compounds keep showing up above the limit in effluent samples: diclofenac and carbamazepine. Both are well-known hard-to-degrade molecules, and our standard aerobic biology simply does not break them down enough. We have done some reading on ozonation and activated carbon polishing, but we have no in-house experience with either. Our process engineer ran a small-scale ozone contact test last autumn and got inconsistent results — partial removal some days, almost none others. We suspect the matrix is interfering but we do not know why. Our lab can measure the compounds by HPLC if we send samples to an external lab, which costs money and takes a week. Budget for a technical study is modest — around 15 000 EUR — and we cannot afford a large pilot rig without external co-funding. A good outcome would be a validated small-scale method we can build into a compact polishing stage that fits within the existing footprint at that client's site.
